chapter_theme: The last ten pairs each wish with the practice its seeker never leaves off: rising with lofty speech, growth with renown, learning with reverence, steadfastness with penance, a good life with deliberation, plenty with toil, safety with just rule and love with hinted speech, and in its centre it sets pleasure and pain each as the price of the other.

91.reading: Someone who wants to rise high is said not to give up lofty speech.
91.nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 91 is line 2 alone. உயர்மொழி may be one's own elevated, worthy speech or the high words of the great that one heeds; the line does not say whose words they are. தண்டான் is read through the ten as 'does not leave off, does not slacken in'; each line pairs a goal with the practice its seeker never drops.

items.claim: lofty speech is not given up by one who wants to rise

92.reading: Someone who wants to grow great is said not to leave off winning wide renown.
92.nuance: வீங்கல் is swelling or growing large, a bodily verb used of fortune; பல்புகழ், 'many-fold fame', suggests renown gathered from many deeds rather than one, so the line asks for a steady run of creditable acts.

items.claim: the many kinds of renown are not let go by one who wants to swell in greatness

93.reading: Someone who wants to learn is said not to slacken in reverent service.
93.nuance: வழிபாடு is worship and devoted service; the line does not name the teacher, but in a saying about learning the one served is most naturally the teacher or the learned. It makes reverence a means of learning, not a reward for it.

items.claim: reverent attendance is never dropped by one who wants to learn

94.reading: Someone who wants to stand firm is said not to leave off doing penance.
94.nuance: நிற்றல், 'standing', is left without an object: it may be steadfastness in one's path, lasting in the world, or remaining in a higher state. தவம் is the renouncer's discipline, so the line is read as addressed to him, though the frame addresses everyone.

items.claim: doing penance is not given up by one who wants to stand firm

95.reading: Someone who wants a good life is said not to leave off careful deliberation.
95.nuance: வாழ்க்கை can be living in general or the life of the household; சூழ்ச்சி is the weighing of means that the Kural assigns to ministers, here required of anyone who wants to make a life.

items.claim: deliberation is never abandoned by one who wants to live well

96.reading: Someone who wants abundance is said not to shrink from toil.
96.nuance: மிகுதி is surplus, more than enough; வருத்தம் is pain of effort, the same word the Kural uses for the body's strain in labour.

items.claim: hard toil is not shunned by one who wants plenty

97.reading: Someone who wants pleasure is said not to shun the pain that comes with it.
97.nuance: Read with the ten's predicate, the line makes pain the price a seeker of pleasure keeps paying; 98 reverses the pair, so the two lines together say each brings the other.

items.claim: pain is not shunned by one who wants pleasure

98.reading: Someone who wants pain, the line says in reverse of 97, does not hold back from pleasure.
98.nuance: Taken literally the saying is a paradox; on the reading taken here it names the unchecked pleasure-seeker by where he ends, since pleasure pursued without stop brings pain. A reading in which the one who seeks hardship (as in penance) still does not refuse all pleasure is possible, but the mirror of 97 favours the first.

items.claim: pleasure is not held back from by one who, in effect, wants pain

99.reading: Someone who wants security is said not to leave off acting by just order.
99.domain_note: the ruler, whose safety the line ties to just rule
99.nuance: ஏமம் is safety or protection; முறை is the word for justice done by a ruler, so the seeker of security is most plausibly the king, though the line does not name him and a householder's fair dealing is a possible wider reading.

items.claim: acting justly is not given up by one who wants safety

100.reading: Someone who wants love is said not to give up speaking by hints.
100.nuance: குறிப்புச்சொல் is words that suggest rather than state; the line makes indirection the lover's constant practice, the last of the ten and the only one in the akam field.

items.claim: speech by hint is not given up by one who wants love

links.note: Line 10 ranks not dwindling later above swelling at first; 92 says the one who wants to swell does not leave off gathering renown.
links.teaches: Read together, the two lines say that greatness is kept from shrinking only by an unbroken run of creditable deeds, so the unslackening of the last ten is the answer to the dwindling feared in the first.

links.note: Line 8 ranks revering the learned above one's own learning; 93 makes unbroken reverent service the condition of learning at all.
links.teaches: The first ten treats reverence as a value above learning and the last treats it as the road to learning, so the book holds both that service is the means and that it outranks the end.

links.note: Kural 395 says the learned learnt by standing before those who know as the poor stand yearning before the rich; 93 says the would-be learner never drops வழிபாடு.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the learner's posture as a beggar's longing, and the line gives it as worship that never lapses, so the pair shows humility in learning as both a hunger and a sustained service.
links.list_adds: In a ten that pairs each goal with the practice its seeker never drops, reverence is set beside toil for plenty and penance for steadfastness, so it reads as the price of learning, where the couplet uses it to rank the learned above the unlearned.

links.note: Kural 265 says penance is pursued here because it gains whatever one wishes, as one wishes; 94 names one such wish, to stand firm, and says its seeker never leaves off penance.
links.teaches: The couplet makes penance a means to any wish at all, while the line ties it to one wish and requires it without a break, so the pair moves from penance's open promise to its continuing cost.
links.list_adds: It sets penance among nine other practices each tied to its own goal, so penance becomes one specialised means among learning, toil and justice rather than the universal means the couplet makes it.

links.note: Kural 671 says deliberation ends in resolve and that delay after resolving is an evil; 95 says the one who wants a good life never leaves off deliberation.
links.teaches: For a single task the couplet closes deliberation once resolved, and for a whole life the line keeps it always open, so the pair shows deliberation ending task by task while never ending as a habit of living.
links.list_adds: It carries சூழ்ச்சி from the minister's work on one undertaking, where the couplet places it, to the making of a whole life, by setting it in a list of lifelong practices.

links.note: Kural 619 says effort yields its wage of bodily strain even where fate will not grant the end; 96 says one who wants plenty does not shun வருத்தம்.
links.teaches: The line makes toil necessary for plenty and the couplet makes it rewarding even against fate, so the pair gives both halves: there is no abundance without strain, and strain is never wholly unpaid.
links.list_adds: Among goals and their unbroken practices, the list makes toil the specific price of surplus, beside pain as the price of pleasure, a pairing of goal and cost the couplet's defence of effort against fate does not make.

links.note: Kural 628 says the one who does not desire pleasure and takes suffering as natural is never distressed; 97 says the one who wants pleasure does not shun pain.
links.teaches: Both bind pain to the pursuit of pleasure, but the couplet frees the man who stops desiring pleasure while the line binds the man who keeps desiring it, so the pair gives the two exits from the same bond.
links.list_adds: Placed beside its mirror in 98, the line makes pleasure and pain each the cost of the other, a symmetrical turn the couplet, which speaks of only one direction, lacks.

links.note: 97 says the seeker of pleasure does not shun pain; 98 reverses the terms, so the seeker of pain does not hold back from pleasure.
links.teaches: Taken as a pair the two lines say the same truth from both sides: pleasure and pain are tied so closely that whoever chases either is pursuing the other.

links.note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure while suffering mounts, and the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; 98 names the unchecked pleasure-seeker as one who in effect wants pain.
links.teaches: The quatrain describes the wise seeing pain inside pleasure, and the line describes what follows when that is not seen, so the pair joins the renouncer's insight to the verdict it passes on the one who lacks it.
links.list_adds: The line compresses the quatrain's contrast of fool and sage into a single reversed formula, and its mirroring with 97 makes the point by form alone, without the quatrain's turn to renunciation.

links.note: Kural 547 says the king protects the world and just order (முறை) protects the king when he keeps it without fail; 99 says the one who wants safety does not leave off acting by just order.
links.teaches: The couplet explains why the king's safety lies in justice and the line states it as an unbroken practice, so the pair shows justice as the ruler's own shelter and not only a duty owed to the ruled.
links.list_adds: It puts the king's justice in a list where each seeker keeps a practice for his own end, so just rule is framed as what the ruler does for his own security, the same way the learner keeps reverence.

links.note: Purananuru 35 counsels Killivalavan that in a land of just rule, where the humble can reach the king when they seek முறை, rain comes when sought, and that if he protects his people the unsubmitting will bow; 99 states the bare rule that security needs just order.
links.teaches: The poem shows to a named Chola what just rule looks like and what it brings, the king reached by the humble and the enemy bowing, and the line reduces the same counsel to a maxim any ruler can carry.

links.note: Kural 1097 says small words without real anger and hostile looks are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant; 100 says the one who wants love does not give up hinted speech.
links.teaches: The line says the lover speaks by hint and the couplet shows how hints are read, even harsh ones turned inside out, so the pair gives both the speaker's practice and the hearer's skill.
links.list_adds: It closes a ten of public goals and their practices with love and its indirection, so hinting stands beside justice and toil as a discipline, where the couplet treats it as a sign within the lovers' scene.

source_issues: 91: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (ஓங்கல் வேண்டுவோன் உயர்மொழி தண்டான்), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.
